div.head: I Cn 2
div.ab: And Godes cyrican griðian ⁊ friðian ⁊ gelomlice secean saulum to hæle ⁊ us sylfum to þearfe.
And witan Godes cyrican griþian ⁊ friþian ⁊ gelomlice seacean us sylfum to þearfe.
[2] And uton Godes cirican griðian ⁊ friðian ⁊ gelomlice secan us silfan to þearfe.
Et sanctam Dei ęcclesiam pacificare, custodire, frequentare ad nostram semper utilitatem satagamus (gaudeamus).
que salute corporis et animę suę.
et Dei ecclesiam tutarentur, pacificarent et frequentarent.
And [uton] Godes cyrican griðian ⁊ friðian ⁊ gelomlice secean saulum to hæle ⁊ us sylfum to þearfe.
And uton Godes cyrican griðian and friðian, and gelomlice secean saulum to hæle and us sylfum to þearfe.
und lasst uns Gottes Kirchen mit Schutzgewalt und Friedensrecht umgeben und häufig besuchen den Seelen zum Heile und uns selbst zu Nutze.
and let us protect and keep the peace of God's churches and visit them often, for the salvation of souls and for our own benefit.
And let us maintain the security and sanctity of the churches of God, and frequently attend them for the salvation of our souls and our own benefit.
And let us respect the peace and sanctity of God’s churches, and regularly attend them for the salvation of our souls and our own benefit.

Vgl. Cn 1020, 19. I Cn 19

Weltliche Gesetze befördern das Seelenheil der Menschen, die deutlich als jetzt lebend gemeint sind; Ine Pro. I Em Pro. IV Eg 15. Hier dagegen, wo ‘uns selbst’ im Ggs. steht, ist vielleicht das Seelenheil Verstorbener gemeint. Jedenfalls nicht Cnuts Seele allein, wie Inst versteht. Diese Zufügung ward in gi gemacht; Ld kann sie aus G haben

Secular laws promote the salvation of the souls of men who are clearly meant as now living; Ine Pro. I Em Pro. IV Eg 15. Here, on the other hand, where ‘ourselves’ stands in contrast, the salvation of the souls of the dead is perhaps meant. At any rate not Cnut’s soul alone, as Inst understands it. This addition was made in gi; Ld may have it from G
Cf. with cap. 2 ff. Insts. of Polity, cap. 25, ed. Thorpe, Anc. Laws, ii. p. 339 f.
Cf. cap. 4; VI Atr. 42. Is cyrican to be taken as plural or with the Latin texts (ecclesiam) as singular? The following clause rather favours the former interpretation.
Cf. Procl. of 1020, cap. 19.
Inst. reads: pro quiete et stabilitate regni sui proque salute corporis et animae suae (i.e. the king’s).
